html:
The trial of Adolf Eichmann was held in Jerusalem from April to December 1961, with his execution in 1962. He was tried in an Israeli court for his part in the Holocaust, after the Mossad capture in Argentina.

Attorney General Gideon Hausner led the prosecution. He chose to build the case around the voices of more than a hundred survivors, not only documents, so that the world heard what happened in the camps and ghettos. The proceedings were filmed and broadcast. Eichmann sat in a glass booth and argued that he was a small official who followed orders, and that he had not decided policy. The judges did not accept this.

In December 1961 he was found guilty on fifteen counts, including crimes against the Jewish people and crimes against humanity, and sentenced to death. The Supreme Court rejected his appeal, and he was hanged near Ramla on 31 May 1962. His body was cremated and the ashes scattered at sea outside Israeli waters. It remains the only civilian execution Israel has carried out.

The trial changed how the Holocaust was discussed. Many young Israelis and others heard survivors for the first time. Hannah Arendt covered it for The New Yorker and coined the phrase "the banality of evil", which is still debated. It also followed the earlier Nuremberg trials.
